posts.title: Making the Web a Better Place: A Conversational Guide to Steve Krug's Usability Wisdom
posts.description: Have you ever visited a website looking for something simple—like a store's phone number or a product price—only to find yourself trapped in a digital maze?
posts.content:
Have you ever visited a website looking for something simple—like a store's phone number or a product price—only to find yourself trapped in a digital maze of pop-ups, confusing menus, and dead ends? You feel your blood pressure rising with each click, and eventually, you just close the tab in frustration, vowing never to return.

This exact experience is what Steve Krug set out to eliminate in his classic book, "Don't Make Me Think!" First published in 2000 and updated several times since, this book isn't a dense technical manual filled with jargon. Instead, it's a refreshingly practical, common-sense approach to creating websites that people actually enjoy using.

Krug's central message is deceptively simple: good usability is invisible. When a website works well, users don't notice the design—they simply accomplish what they came to do and leave satisfied. It's only when things go wrong that users become painfully aware of the interface standing between them and their goals.

Don't Make Me Think!

This is Krug's First Law of Usability. The goal is simple: when someone looks at your webpage, it should be self-evident. They should understand what the page is, what they can do there, and how to do it—without spending a single millisecond consciously thinking about it.

But on the web, we constantly create tiny question marks in users' heads: using cute names for navigation links, hiding the search bar, making buttons that don't look like buttons, using industry jargon. Each micro-frustration drains the user's energy and patience, pushing them closer to the back button.

How We Really Use the Web

Here's a truth that might hurt: most designers build websites as if users are going to read every word. The reality? Users don't read websites—they scan them. Krug identifies three key behaviors:

1. We Scan, Not Read

We look for visual or textual clues that tell us we're on the right track. Headlines, bold text, bullet points, and images act like signposts.

2. We Satisfice

We don't weigh all options to find the best choice. We click the first reasonable-looking option we see because the penalty for being wrong is usually just hitting the Back button.

3. We Muddle Through

We don't read instructions. We just forge ahead, clicking things and seeing what happens.

Billboard Design 101

Since users are whizzing by your site like a car going 60 miles per hour, you need to design pages like billboards. Five key strategies:

1. Create a Clear Visual Hierarchy

The most important elements should be the most prominent. Logically related items should be grouped together.

2. Take Advantage of Conventions

Don't reinvent the wheel. Logo top-left, navigation across the top, search in the top-right. Conventions exist because they work.

3. Break Pages Into Clearly Defined Areas

Divide your page into distinct zones so users can instantly decide what to focus on and what to safely ignore.

4. Make Clickable Elements Obvious

Buttons that look raised, links that are underlined, hover states that show interactivity.

5. Minimize Noise

Every unnecessary element competes for the user's limited attention. If it doesn't serve a clear purpose, remove it.

Omit Needless Words

Krug's Third Law: Get rid of half the words on each page, then get rid of half of what's left. Happy talk, instructions, redundancy — all of it goes. Cutting words reduces clutter, makes useful content stand out, and respects your users' time.

Navigation IS the Website

Without good navigation, users are inherently lost. Every page needs: a site ID (your logo), a clear page name, you-are-here indicators, and breadcrumbs.

Test Early and Often

Krug's core insight: Testing one user is 100% better than testing none. You don't need a fancy lab. Test 3-4 users, once a month, spend a morning watching them complete tasks. That's it.

Conclusion

Usability is simply common sense. It's about empathy — realizing that your users are busy, distracted, and have better things to do than solve the puzzle of your interface. Make things obvious. Use clear labels. Create visual hierarchy. Test with real people. Don't make your users think.

posts.title: Thinking, Fast and Slow: A Practical Guide to Daniel Kahneman's Masterpiece
posts.description: Why do smart people make dumb decisions? Explore System 1 vs System 2, cognitive biases, anchoring, loss aversion, and the hidden forces shaping every choice you make.
posts.content:
Have you ever bought something late at night and wondered the next morning, "Why on earth did I buy that?" Or found yourself assuming someone is smart just because they're good-looking? Or felt terrified of flying even though you know, statistically, driving is far more dangerous?

Welcome to the messy, fascinating, and often irrational world of human decision-making.

In 2011, Daniel Kahneman — a psychologist who won the Nobel Prize in Economics — published Thinking, Fast and Slow. After decades of research, Kahneman revealed something profound: we don't think the way we think we think.

The Two Characters Living in Your Mind

Kahneman calls them System 1 and System 2 — and understanding the difference is the master key that unlocks everything else in this book.

System 1: The Fast Thinker

System 1 is your brain's autopilot. Fast, automatic, emotional, operating with almost no effort. It instantly recognizes anger on someone's face, knows 2+2=4 without thinking, reads words on a billboard without trying. It's always on. You can't turn it off.

But System 1 loves shortcuts. It makes snap judgments based on patterns and gut feelings — not careful analysis. And those shortcuts can lead to spectacular errors.

System 2: The Slow Thinker

System 2 is the careful analyst. Slow, deliberate, logical. It multiplies 17×24 in your head, fills out a complex tax form, resists the temptation to eat dessert on a diet. But here's what Kahneman discovered: System 2 is lazy. It often just accepts whatever System 1 suggests without verifying it.

Anchoring: How Random Numbers Shape Your Judgments

When you estimate a value, your brain anchors on whatever number was mentioned recently — even if it's completely irrelevant.

In one study, researchers asked people how much they'd pay to save 50,000 birds. With no anchor: $64. When first asked "Would you pay $5?": $20. When first asked "Would you pay $400?": $143. Same question, different anchors, wildly different answers.

CRO application: Use strikethrough pricing. Showing "$150 → $100" makes $100 feel like a win because $150 acts as an anchor.

Loss Aversion: Losses Hurt Twice as Much as Gains Feel Good

The pain of losing $100 is about twice as intense as the joy of winning $100. This is Prospect Theory — and it has profound implications for how you frame offers.

"Don't lose your $50 discount" is more powerful than "Save $50." Free trials work because once users have the product, losing it hurts more than the subscription cost.

The Availability Bias: Vivid Events Feel More Likely

We judge the frequency of events by how easily we can think of examples. Plane crashes are dramatic, memorable, and heavily covered — so they feel more dangerous than driving, even though statistically driving is far worse.

CRO application: One vivid negative review can outweigh 50 positive ones. Use specific, concrete testimonials — a story about one person saving $1,000 is more "available" to the mind than a vague claim.

Framing: The Same Fact, Presented Differently

A surgery with a "90% survival rate" sounds much better than one with a "10% mortality rate" — even though they're identical. We're not reality-bound; we're frame-bound.

"90% Fat-Free" sounds better than "10% Fat." "Investing in your future" sounds better than "spending $20 a month." Frame strategically.

Putting It All Together

Understanding these biases doesn't mean you can eliminate them — Kahneman himself admits he still falls for the same traps he spent decades studying. But understanding them gives you something valuable: the ability to recognize when they're happening and create systems that work with your mind rather than against it.

The goal isn't to become a perfectly rational robot. It's to understand the beautiful, messy, irrational machine that is the human mind — and learn to work with it.

posts.title: You Can Stop Your A/B Test Early. Here's How to Do It Without Cheating
posts.description: How a wartime statistician's insight became the backbone of modern A/B testing - and why CRO teams who still wait for fixed sample sizes are leaving growth on the table.
posts.content:
There's a particular kind of anxiety that every CRO specialist knows well. You've launched an experiment. You refresh the dashboard. The numbers look promising — variant B is up 18% on conversions. Your Slack is pinging. Your CEO is asking questions.

And then comes the uncomfortable truth: the test isn't done yet.

So what do you do? Do you call it early and risk being wrong? Do you wait the full two weeks? Or do you peek at the results just this once — promising yourself it doesn't count?

Here's the thing: that dilemma is not a personal failing. It's a fundamental limitation of the way classical A/B testing was designed. And it's precisely the problem that Sequential Testing was built to solve.

The Problem With "Wait Until the End"

Traditional A/B testing follows a fixed-horizon design. You decide in advance how many users you need, you wait until you've collected that many, and then — and only then — you look at the results.

The problem is that almost nobody actually does this. In practice, teams check dashboards daily. They peek at conversion rates after the first 500 visitors. And this behavior — completely natural, completely human — breaks the math.

Every time you look at your data and consider making a decision, you create a new opportunity for a false positive. Look ten times at noisy data, and your actual false positive rate might be 30% — even though you set your threshold at 5%. This is called the peeking problem.

A Statistician in Wartime

The concept that would eventually fix this problem didn't come from Silicon Valley. It came from World War II.

In the early 1940s, a mathematician named Abraham Wald was working with a classified unit of American researchers solving military problems with data. One problem: how do you test whether artillery shells meet standards — without having to destroy thousands of them?

In 1945, Wald published the Sequential Probability Ratio Test (SPRT). Instead of committing to a sample size upfront, you test continuously and update a likelihood ratio — a running score of the evidence. When that score crosses a threshold in either direction, you stop. Mathematically rigorous. Valid at any sample size.

Four Methods, Four Philosophies

1. Pocock (1977)

Sets the same significance threshold at every look. Simple and predictable — great for teams that want scheduled checkpoints at 25%, 50%, 75%, and 100%.

2. O'Brien-Fleming (1979)

Extremely conservative at early looks, relaxing toward a standard threshold at the final analysis. The gold standard in clinical trials. Best for high-stakes experiments where false positives are very costly.

3. Alpha Spending (Lan-DeMets, 1983)

You have a total alpha budget of 0.05. Spend it however you like, but track how much you've used. Genuinely flexible monitoring — check whenever you want. This is why platforms like Statsig and Optimizely use it.

4. mSPRT — Wald's Modern Descendant

Truly always-valid. Uses a likelihood ratio called the E-value (Λ). You stop when Λ ≥ 1/α. This threshold is valid at any sample size, at any time, with any monitoring frequency. You can literally check every hour and the math is still correct.

What This Means for CRO

CRO is fundamentally a game of iteration speed. The team that runs 200 experiments in a year will learn more — and compound those learnings more effectively — than the team that runs 50.

With sequential testing properly implemented, tests can stop early when the effect is real (saving 30-40% of planned sample) or stop for futility when there's no effect (saving traffic for the next experiment). Across a year of testing, this can translate to a 30–50% increase in experiments run — without any additional traffic.

A Tool I Built

Understanding sequential testing conceptually is one thing. Applying it in practice requires mathematical infrastructure most teams don't have. That's why I built the A/B Test Group Sequential Calculator — a browser-based tool covering all four methods, giving you actionable decisions, not just numbers.

No API keys. No account. Runs entirely in the browser. Try it in the middle of your next test review.

Conclusion

Sequential testing isn't just a statistical technique. It's a philosophy: make decisions when the evidence is ready, not when a calendar says so.

The peeking problem isn't solved by willpower. It's solved by using methods that were designed for a world where people actually look at their dashboards. The answer, it turns out, is a boundary. And it was set before the experiment began.
